# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/auto_awq.md "Edit this page")

> ⚠️ **Warning:** The `AutoAWQ` library is deprecated. This functionality has been adopted by the vLLM project in [`llm-compressor`](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/tree/main/examples/awq). For the recommended quantization workflow, please see the AWQ examples in [`llm-compressor`](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/tree/main/examples/awq). For more details on the deprecation, refer to the original [AutoAWQ repository](https://github.com/casper-hansen/AutoAWQ).

To create a new 4-bit quantized model, you can leverage [AutoAWQ](https://github.com/casper-hansen/AutoAWQ). Quantization reduces the model's precision from BF16/FP16 to INT4 which effectively reduces the total model memory footprint. The main benefits are lower latency and memory usage.

You can quantize your own models by installing AutoAWQ or picking one of the [6500+ models on Huggingface](https://huggingface.co/models?search=awq).

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)pip install autoawq`

After installing AutoAWQ, you are ready to quantize a model. Please refer to the [AutoAWQ documentation](https://casper-hansen.github.io/AutoAWQ/examples/#basic-quantization) for further details. Here is an example of how to quantize `mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2`:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)from awq import AutoAWQForCausalLM [](#__codelineno-1-2)from transformers import AutoTokenizer [](#__codelineno-1-3)[](#__codelineno-1-4)model_path = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2" [](#__codelineno-1-5)quant_path = "mistral-instruct-v0.2-awq" [](#__codelineno-1-6)quant_config = {"zero_point": True, "q_group_size": 128, "w_bit": 4, "version": "GEMM"} [](#__codelineno-1-7)[](#__codelineno-1-8)# Load model [](#__codelineno-1-9)model = AutoAWQForCausalLM.from_pretrained(     [](#__codelineno-1-10)    model_path,    [](#__codelineno-1-11)    low_cpu_mem_usage=True,    [](#__codelineno-1-12)    use_cache=False, [](#__codelineno-1-13)) [](#__codelineno-1-14)tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path, trust_remote_code=True) [](#__codelineno-1-15)[](#__codelineno-1-16)# Quantize [](#__codelineno-1-17)model.quantize(tokenizer, quant_config=quant_config) [](#__codelineno-1-18)[](#__codelineno-1-19)# Save quantized model [](#__codelineno-1-20)model.save_quantized(quant_path) [](#__codelineno-1-21)tokenizer.save_pretrained(quant_path) [](#__codelineno-1-22)[](#__codelineno-1-23)print(f'Model is quantized and saved at "{quant_path}"')`

To run an AWQ model with vLLM, you can use [TheBloke/Llama-2-7b-Chat-AWQ](https://huggingface.co/TheBloke/Llama-2-7b-Chat-AWQ) with the following command:

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)python examples/deployment/llm_engine_example.py \     [](#__codelineno-2-2)    --model TheBloke/Llama-2-7b-Chat-AWQ \    [](#__codelineno-2-3)    --quantization awq`

AWQ models are also supported directly through the LLM entrypoint:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-3-2)[](#__codelineno-3-3)# Sample prompts. [](#__codelineno-3-4)prompts = [     [](#__codelineno-3-5)    "Hello, my name is",    [](#__codelineno-3-6)    "The president of the United States is",    [](#__codelineno-3-7)    "The capital of France is",    [](#__codelineno-3-8)    "The future of AI is", [](#__codelineno-3-9)] [](#__codelineno-3-10)# Create a sampling params object. [](#__codelineno-3-11)sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95) [](#__codelineno-3-12)[](#__codelineno-3-13)# Create an LLM. [](#__codelineno-3-14)llm = LLM(model="TheBloke/Llama-2-7b-Chat-AWQ", quantization="AWQ") [](#__codelineno-3-15)# Generate texts from the prompts. The output is a list of RequestOutput objects [](#__codelineno-3-16)# that contain the prompt, generated text, and other information. [](#__codelineno-3-17)outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params) [](#__codelineno-3-18)# Print the outputs. [](#__codelineno-3-19)for output in outputs:     [](#__codelineno-3-20)    prompt = output.prompt    [](#__codelineno-3-21)    generated_text = output.outputs[0].text    [](#__codelineno-3-22)    print(f"Prompt: {prompt!r}, Generated text: {generated_text!r}")`

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/bnb.md "Edit this page")

vLLM now supports [BitsAndBytes](https://github.com/TimDettmers/bitsandbytes) for more efficient model inference. BitsAndBytes quantizes models to reduce memory usage and enhance performance without significantly sacrificing accuracy. Compared to other quantization methods, BitsAndBytes eliminates the need for calibrating the quantized model with input data.

Below are the steps to utilize BitsAndBytes with vLLM.

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)pip install bitsandbytes>=0.49.2`

vLLM reads the model's config file and supports both in-flight quantization and pre-quantized checkpoint.

You can find bitsandbytes quantized models on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/models?search=bitsandbytes). And usually, these repositories have a config.json file that includes a quantization\_config section.

## Read quantized checkpoint[¶](#read-quantized-checkpoint "Permanent link")

For pre-quantized checkpoints, vLLM will try to infer the quantization method from the config file, so you don't need to explicitly specify the quantization argument.

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-1-2)import torch [](#__codelineno-1-3)# unsloth/tinyllama-bnb-4bit is a pre-quantized checkpoint. [](#__codelineno-1-4)model_id = "unsloth/tinyllama-bnb-4bit" [](#__codelineno-1-5)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-1-6)    model=model_id,    [](#__codelineno-1-7)    dtype=torch.bfloat16,    [](#__codelineno-1-8)    trust_remote_code=True, [](#__codelineno-1-9))`

## Inflight quantization: load as 4bit quantization[¶](#inflight-quantization-load-as-4bit-quantization "Permanent link")

For inflight 4bit quantization with BitsAndBytes, you need to explicitly specify the quantization argument.

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-2-2)import torch [](#__codelineno-2-3)model_id = "huggyllama/llama-7b" [](#__codelineno-2-4)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-2-5)    model=model_id,    [](#__codelineno-2-6)    dtype=torch.bfloat16,    [](#__codelineno-2-7)    trust_remote_code=True,    [](#__codelineno-2-8)    quantization="bitsandbytes", [](#__codelineno-2-9))`

## OpenAI Compatible Server[¶](#openai-compatible-server "Permanent link")

Append the following to your model arguments for 4bit inflight quantization:

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)--quantization bitsandbytes`

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/fp8_vit_attn.md "Edit this page")

For visual understanding workloads with large images (e.g. QHD, 4K) and relatively short text prompts/generation, the ViT encoder attention can become a significant bottleneck, especially when the text model is quantized (e.g. NVFP4). vLLM supports optional FP8 quantization for the ViT encoder attention via the FlashInfer cuDNN backend. Q/K/V are quantized on-the-fly to FP8 before the cuDNN attention call.

Note

-   Currently supports Qwen3-VL family models only (`qwen3_vl`, `qwen3_vl_moe`, `qwen3_5`, `qwen3_5_moe`, and other models using Qwen3 ViT).
-   Dynamic scaling is not compatible with ViT full CUDA graphs.
-   Performance gains are mostly visible at QHD/4K resolutions or multi-image requests. Smaller images may see no speedup due to quantization overhead (3 quantization kernel launches + un-padding).
-   FP8 tensor-core speedup is more pronounced on GB300 than GB200.

## Requirements[¶](#requirements "Permanent link")

-   FlashInfer cuDNN backend with cuDNN >= 9.17.1.

## Usage[¶](#usage "Permanent link")

Enable FP8 ViT attention by passing `--mm-encoder-attn-dtype fp8` together with `--mm-encoder-attn-backend FLASHINFER`:

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)vllm serve $MODEL \     [](#__codelineno-0-2)    --mm-encoder-attn-backend FLASHINFER \    [](#__codelineno-0-3)    --mm-encoder-attn-dtype fp8`

By default (no scale file), **dynamic scaling** is used: a 16-entry circular buffer of observed Q/K/V amax values drives per-forward scale updates. This matches BF16 accuracy without any calibration but adds a small per-forward overhead.

## Calibrate-Once, Reuse Workflow (Recommended)[¶](#calibrate-once-reuse-workflow-recommended "Permanent link")

For production, calibrate static scales on a representative dataset once and reuse them to avoid the dynamic overhead:

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)# Step 1: calibrate and save scales (runs dynamic scaling for 16 passes, [](#__codelineno-1-2)# then dumps the learned scales to JSON). [](#__codelineno-1-3)vllm bench mm-processor \     [](#__codelineno-1-4)    --model $MODEL --mm-encoder-attn-backend FLASHINFER \    [](#__codelineno-1-5)    --mm-encoder-attn-dtype fp8 \    [](#__codelineno-1-6)    --mm-encoder-fp8-scale-save-path /path/to/scales.json \    [](#__codelineno-1-7)    --dataset-name hf --dataset-path lmarena-ai/VisionArena-Chat \    [](#__codelineno-1-8)    --num-prompts 100 [](#__codelineno-1-9)[](#__codelineno-1-10)# Step 2: serve with static scales (no dynamic overhead). [](#__codelineno-1-11)vllm serve $MODEL \     [](#__codelineno-1-12)    --mm-encoder-attn-backend FLASHINFER \    [](#__codelineno-1-13)    --mm-encoder-attn-dtype fp8 \    [](#__codelineno-1-14)    --mm-encoder-fp8-scale-path /path/to/scales.json`

Saved scales are multiplied by `--mm-encoder-fp8-scale-save-margin` (default `1.5`) to leave headroom against activation outliers not present in the calibration set. The default has been validated to generalize across datasets (e.g. VisionArena-Chat calibration maintains BF16 accuracy on ChartQA).

## Scale File Format[¶](#scale-file-format "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-2-1){     [](#__codelineno-2-2)    "visual.blocks.0.attn.attn": {"q": 224.0, "k": 198.0, "v": 210.0},    [](#__codelineno-2-3)    "visual.blocks.1.attn.attn": {"q": 218.0, "k": 195.0, "v": 207.0} [](#__codelineno-2-4)}`

Keys `q_scale` / `k_scale` / `v_scale` are accepted as aliases.

## Performance[¶](#performance "Permanent link")

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/gguf.md "Edit this page")

Warning

Please note that GGUF support in vLLM is highly experimental and under-optimized at the moment, it might be incompatible with other features. Currently, you can use GGUF as a way to reduce memory footprint. If you encounter any issues, please report them to the vLLM team.

Warning

Currently, vllm only supports loading single-file GGUF models. If you have a multi-files GGUF model, you can use [gguf-split](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp/pull/6135) tool to merge them to a single-file model.

To run a GGUF model with vLLM, you can use the `repo_id:quant_type` format to load directly from HuggingFace. For example, to load a Q4\_K\_M quantized model from [unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF):

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)# We recommend using the tokenizer from base model to avoid long-time and buggy tokenizer conversion. [](#__codelineno-0-2)vllm serve unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_K_M --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`

You can also add `--tensor-parallel-size 2` to enable tensor parallelism inference with 2 GPUs:

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)vllm serve unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_K_M \    [](#__codelineno-1-2)   --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \   [](#__codelineno-1-3)   --tensor-parallel-size 2`

Alternatively, you can download and use a local GGUF file:

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)wget https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF/resolve/main/Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf [](#__codelineno-2-2)vllm serve ./Qwen3-0.6B-Q4_K_M.gguf --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`

Warning

We recommend using the tokenizer from base model instead of GGUF model. Because the tokenizer conversion from GGUF is time-consuming and unstable, especially for some models with large vocab size.

GGUF assumes that HuggingFace can convert the metadata to a config file. In case HuggingFace doesn't support your model you can manually create a config and pass it as hf-config-path

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)# If your model is not supported by HuggingFace you can manually provide a HuggingFace compatible config path [](#__codelineno-3-2)vllm serve unsloth/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF:Q4_K_M \    [](#__codelineno-3-3)   --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \   [](#__codelineno-3-4)   --hf-config-path Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B`

You can also use the GGUF model directly through the LLM entrypoint:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-4-2)[](#__codelineno-4-3)# In this script, we demonstrate how to pass input to the chat method: [](#__codelineno-4-4)conversation = [    [](#__codelineno-4-5)   {      [](#__codelineno-4-6)      "role": "system",      [](#__codelineno-4-7)      "content": "You are a helpful assistant",   [](#__codelineno-4-8)   },   [](#__codelineno-4-9)   {      [](#__codelineno-4-10)      "role": "user",      [](#__codelineno-4-11)      "content": "Hello",   [](#__codelineno-4-12)   },   [](#__codelineno-4-13)   {      [](#__codelineno-4-14)      "role": "assistant",      [](#__codelineno-4-15)      "content": "Hello! How can I assist you today?",   [](#__codelineno-4-16)   },   [](#__codelineno-4-17)   {      [](#__codelineno-4-18)      "role": "user",      [](#__codelineno-4-19)      "content": "Write an essay about the importance of higher education.",   [](#__codelineno-4-20)   }, [](#__codelineno-4-21)] [](#__codelineno-4-22)[](#__codelineno-4-23)# Create a sampling params object. # page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/gptqmodel.md "Edit this page")

To create a new 4-bit or 8-bit GPTQ quantized model, you can leverage [GPTQModel](https://github.com/ModelCloud/GPTQModel) from ModelCloud.AI.

Quantization reduces the model's precision from BF16/FP16 (16-bits) to INT4 (4-bits) or INT8 (8-bits) which significantly reduces the total model memory footprint while at-the-same-time increasing inference performance.

Compatible GPTQModel quantized models can leverage the `Marlin` and `Machete` vLLM custom kernels to maximize batching transactions-per-second `tps` and token-latency performance for both Ampere (A100+) and Hopper (H100+) Nvidia GPUs. These two kernels are highly optimized by vLLM and NeuralMagic (now part of Redhat) to allow world-class inference performance of quantized GPTQ models.

GPTQModel is one of the few quantization toolkits in the world that allows `Dynamic` per-module quantization where different layers and/or modules within a llm model can be further optimized with custom quantization parameters. `Dynamic` quantization is fully integrated into vLLM and backed up by support from the ModelCloud.AI team. Please refer to [GPTQModel readme](https://github.com/ModelCloud/GPTQModel?tab=readme-ov-file#dynamic-quantization-per-module-quantizeconfig-override) for more details on this and other advanced features.

## Installation[¶](#installation "Permanent link")

You can quantize your own models by installing [GPTQModel](https://github.com/ModelCloud/GPTQModel) or picking one of the [5000+ models on Huggingface](https://huggingface.co/models?search=gptq).

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)pip install -U gptqmodel --no-build-isolation -v`

## Quantizing a model[¶](#quantizing-a-model "Permanent link")

After installing GPTQModel, you are ready to quantize a model. Please refer to the [GPTQModel readme](https://github.com/ModelCloud/GPTQModel/?tab=readme-ov-file#quantization) for further details.

Here is an example of how to quantize `meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct`:

Code

``[](#__codelineno-1-1)from datasets import load_dataset [](#__codelineno-1-2)from gptqmodel import GPTQModel, QuantizeConfig [](#__codelineno-1-3)[](#__codelineno-1-4)model_id = "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct" [](#__codelineno-1-5)quant_path = "Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct-gptqmodel-4bit" [](#__codelineno-1-6)[](#__codelineno-1-7)calibration_dataset = load_dataset(     [](#__codelineno-1-8)    "allenai/c4",    [](#__codelineno-1-9)    data_files="en/c4-train.00001-of-01024.json.gz",    [](#__codelineno-1-10)    split="train", [](#__codelineno-1-11)).select(range(1024))["text"] [](#__codelineno-1-12)[](#__codelineno-1-13)quant_config = QuantizeConfig(bits=4, group_size=128) [](#__codelineno-1-14)[](#__codelineno-1-15)model = GPTQModel.load(model_id, quant_config) [](#__codelineno-1-16)[](#__codelineno-1-17)# increase `batch_size` to match gpu/vram specs to speed up quantization [](#__codelineno-1-18)model.quantize(calibration_dataset, batch_size=2) [](#__codelineno-1-19)[](#__codelineno-1-20)model.save(quant_path)``

## Running a quantized model with vLLM[¶](#running-a-quantized-model-with-vllm "Permanent link")

To run an GPTQModel quantized model with vLLM, you can use [DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B-gptqmodel-4bit-vortex-v2](https://huggingface.co/ModelCloud/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B-gptqmodel-4bit-vortex-v2) with the following command:

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)python examples/deployment/llm_engine_example.py \     [](#__codelineno-2-2)    --model ModelCloud/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B-gptqmodel-4bit-vortex-v2`

## Using GPTQModel with vLLM's Python API[¶](#using-gptqmodel-with-vllms-python-api "Permanent link")

GPTQModel quantized models are also supported directly through the LLM entrypoint:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-3-2)[](#__codelineno-3-3)# Sample prompts. [](#__codelineno-3-4)prompts = [     [](#__codelineno-3-5)    "Hello, my name is",    [](#__codelineno-3-6)    "The president of the United States is",    [](#__codelineno-3-7)    "The capital of France is",    [](#__codelineno-3-8)    "The future of AI is", [](#__codelineno-3-9)] [](#__codelineno-3-10)[](#__codelineno-3-11)# Create a sampling params object. [](#__codelineno-3-12)sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.6, top_p=0.9) [](#__codelineno-3-13)[](#__codelineno-3-14)# Create an LLM. [](#__codelineno-3-15)llm = LLM(model="ModelCloud/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B-gptqmodel-4bit-vortex-v2") [](#__codelineno-3-16)[](#__codelineno-3-17)# Generate texts from the prompts. The output is a list of RequestOutput objects [](#__codelineno-3-18)# that contain the prompt, generated text, and other information. [](#__codelineno-3-19)outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params) [](#__codelineno-3-20)[](#__codelineno-3-21)# Print the outputs. [](#__codelineno-3-22)print("-"*50) [](#__codelineno-3-23)for output in outputs:     [](#__codelineno-3-24)    prompt = output.prompt    [](#__codelineno-3-25)    generated_text = output.outputs[0].text    [](#__codelineno-3-26)    print(f"Prompt: {prompt!r}\nGenerated text: {generated_text!r}")    [](#__codelineno-3-27)    print("-"*50)`

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/inc.md "Edit this page")

[AutoRound](https://github.com/intel/auto-round) is Intel’s advanced quantization algorithm designed for large language models(LLMs). It produces highly efficient **INT2, INT3, INT4, INT8, MXFP8, MXFP4, NVFP4**, and **GGUF** quantized models, balancing accuracy and inference performance. AutoRound is also part of the [Intel® Neural Compressor](https://github.com/intel/neural-compressor). For a deeper introduction, see the [AutoRound step-by-step guide](https://github.com/intel/auto-round/blob/main/docs/step_by_step.md).

## Key Features[¶](#key-features "Permanent link")

✅ Superior Accuracy Delivers strong performance even at 2–3 bits [example models](https://huggingface.co/collections/OPEA/2-3-bits)

✅ Fast Mixed `Bits`/`Dtypes` Scheme Generation Automatically configure in minutes

✅ Support for exporting **AutoRound, AutoAWQ, AutoGPTQ, and GGUF** formats

✅ **10+ vision-language models (VLMs)** are supported

✅ **Per-layer mixed-bit quantization** for fine-grained control

✅ **RTN (Round-To-Nearest) mode** for quick quantization with slight accuracy loss

✅ **Multiple quantization recipes**: best, base, and light

✅ Advanced utilities such as immediate packing and support for **10+ backends**

## Supported Recipes on Intel Platforms[¶](#supported-recipes-on-intel-platforms "Permanent link")

On Intel platforms, AutoRound recipes are being enabled progressively by format and hardware. Currently, vLLM supports:

-   **`W4A16`**: weight-only, 4-bit weights with 16-bit activations
-   **`W8A16`**: weight-only, 8-bit weights with 16-bit activations

Additional recipes and formats will be supported in future releases.

## Quantizing a Model[¶](#quantizing-a-model "Permanent link")

### Installation[¶](#installation "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)uv pip install auto-round`

### Quantize with CLI[¶](#quantize-with-cli "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)auto-round \     [](#__codelineno-1-2)    --model Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B \    [](#__codelineno-1-3)    --scheme W4A16 \    [](#__codelineno-1-4)    --format auto_round \    [](#__codelineno-1-5)    --output_dir ./tmp_autoround`

### Quantize with Python API[¶](#quantize-with-python-api "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer [](#__codelineno-2-2)from auto_round import AutoRound [](#__codelineno-2-3)[](#__codelineno-2-4)model_name = "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" [](#__codelineno-2-5)autoround = AutoRound(model_name, scheme="W4A16") [](#__codelineno-2-6)[](#__codelineno-2-7)# the best accuracy, 4-5X slower, low_gpu_mem_usage could save ~20G but ~30% slower [](#__codelineno-2-8)# autoround = AutoRound(model, tokenizer, nsamples=512, iters=1000, low_gpu_mem_usage=True, bits=bits, group_size=group_size, sym=sym) [](#__codelineno-2-9)[](#__codelineno-2-10)# 2-3X speedup, slight accuracy drop at W4G128 [](#__codelineno-2-11)# autoround = AutoRound(model, tokenizer, nsamples=128, iters=50, lr=5e-3, bits=bits, group_size=group_size, sym=sym ) [](#__codelineno-2-12)[](#__codelineno-2-13)output_dir = "./tmp_autoround" [](#__codelineno-2-14)# format= 'auto_round'(default), 'auto_gptq', 'auto_awq' [](#__codelineno-2-15)autoround.quantize_and_save(output_dir, format="auto_round")`

## Deploying AutoRound Quantized Models in vLLM[¶](#deploying-autoround-quantized-models-in-vllm "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)vllm serve Intel/DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B-int4-AutoRound \     [](#__codelineno-3-2)    --gpu-memory-utilization 0.8 \    [](#__codelineno-3-3)    --max-model-len 4096`

Note

To deploy `wNa16` models on Intel GPU/CPU, please add `--enforce-eager` for now.

## Evaluating the Quantized Model with vLLM[¶](#evaluating-the-quantized-model-with-vllm "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)lm_eval --model vllm \   [](#__codelineno-4-2)  --model_args pretrained="Intel/DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B-int4-AutoRound,max_model_len=8192,max_num_batched_tokens=32768,max_num_seqs=128,gpu_memory_utilization=0.8,dtype=bfloat16,max_gen_toks=2048,enforce_eager=True" \  [](#__codelineno-4-3)  --tasks gsm8k \  [](#__codelineno-4-4)  --num_fewshot 5 \  [](#__codelineno-4-5)  --batch_size 128`

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/modelopt.md "Edit this page")

The [NVIDIA Model Optimizer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Model-Optimizer) is a library designed to optimize models for inference with NVIDIA GPUs. It includes tools for Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) and Quantization Aware Training (QAT) of Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision Language Models (VLMs), and diffusion models.

We recommend installing the library with:

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)pip install nvidia-modelopt`

## Supported ModelOpt checkpoint formats[¶](#supported-modelopt-checkpoint-formats "Permanent link")

vLLM detects ModelOpt checkpoints via `hf_quant_config.json` and supports the following `quantization.quant_algo` values:

-   `FP8`: per-tensor weight scale (+ optional static activation scale).
-   `FP8_PER_CHANNEL_PER_TOKEN`: per-channel weight scale and dynamic per-token activation quantization.
-   `FP8_PB_WO` (ModelOpt may emit `fp8_pb_wo`): block-scaled FP8 weight-only (typically 128×128 blocks).
-   `NVFP4`: ModelOpt NVFP4 checkpoints (use `quantization="modelopt_fp4"`).
-   `MXFP8`: ModelOpt MXFP8 checkpoints (use `quantization="modelopt_mxfp8"`).

## Quantizing HuggingFace Models with PTQ[¶](#quantizing-huggingface-models-with-ptq "Permanent link")

You can quantize HuggingFace models using the example scripts provided in the Model Optimizer repository. The primary script for LLM PTQ is typically found within the `examples/llm_ptq` directory.

Below is an example showing how to quantize a model using modelopt's PTQ API:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)import modelopt.torch.quantization as mtq [](#__codelineno-1-2)from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM [](#__codelineno-1-3)[](#__codelineno-1-4)# Load the model from HuggingFace [](#__codelineno-1-5)model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("<path_or_model_id>") [](#__codelineno-1-6)[](#__codelineno-1-7)# Select the quantization config, for example, FP8 [](#__codelineno-1-8)config = mtq.FP8_DEFAULT_CFG [](#__codelineno-1-9)[](#__codelineno-1-10)# Define a forward loop function for calibration [](#__codelineno-1-11)def forward_loop(model):     [](#__codelineno-1-12)    for data in calib_set:        [](#__codelineno-1-13)        model(data) [](#__codelineno-1-14)[](#__codelineno-1-15)# PTQ with in-place replacement of quantized modules [](#__codelineno-1-16)model = mtq.quantize(model, config, forward_loop)`

After the model is quantized, you can export it to a quantized checkpoint using the export API:

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)import torch [](#__codelineno-2-2)from modelopt.torch.export import export_hf_checkpoint [](#__codelineno-2-3)[](#__codelineno-2-4)with torch.inference_mode():     [](#__codelineno-2-5)    export_hf_checkpoint(        [](#__codelineno-2-6)        model,  # The quantized model.        [](#__codelineno-2-7)        export_dir,  # The directory where the exported files will be stored.    [](#__codelineno-2-8)    )`

The quantized checkpoint can then be deployed with vLLM. As an example, the following code shows how to deploy `nvidia/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-FP8`, which is the FP8 quantized checkpoint derived from `meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct`, using vLLM:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-3-2)[](#__codelineno-3-3)def main():     [](#__codelineno-3-4)    model_id = "nvidia/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-FP8" [](#__codelineno-3-5)    [](#__codelineno-3-6)    # Ensure you specify quantization="modelopt" when loading the modelopt checkpoint    [](#__codelineno-3-7)    llm = LLM(model=model_id, quantization="modelopt", trust_remote_code=True) [](#__codelineno-3-8)    [](#__codelineno-3-9)    sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.9) [](#__codelineno-3-10)    [](#__codelineno-3-11)    prompts = [        [](#__codelineno-3-12)        "Hello, my name is",        [](#__codelineno-3-13)        "The president of the United States is",        [](#__codelineno-3-14)        "The capital of France is",        [](#__codelineno-3-15)        "The future of AI is",    [](#__codelineno-3-16)    ] [](#__codelineno-3-17)    [](#__codelineno-3-18)    outputs = llm.generate(prompts, sampling_params) [](#__codelineno-3-19)    [](#__codelineno-3-20)    for output in outputs:        [](#__codelineno-3-21)        prompt = output.prompt        [](#__codelineno-3-22)        generated_text = output.outputs[0].text        [](#__codelineno-3-23)        print(f"Prompt: {prompt!r}, Generated text: {generated_text!r}") [](#__codelineno-3-24)[](#__codelineno-3-25)if __name__ == "__main__":     [](#__codelineno-3-26)    main()`

## Running the OpenAI-compatible server[¶](#running-the-openai-compatible-server "Permanent link")

To serve a local ModelOpt checkpoint via the OpenAI-compatible API:

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)vllm serve <path_to_exported_checkpoint> \   [](#__codelineno-4-2)  --quantization modelopt \  [](#__codelineno-4-3)  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000`

## Testing (local checkpoints)[¶](#testing-local-checkpoints "Permanent link")

vLLM's ModelOpt unit tests are gated by local checkpoint paths and are skipped by default in CI. To run the tests locally:

`[](#__codelineno-5-1)export VLLM_TEST_MODELOPT_FP8_PC_PT_MODEL_PATH=<path_to_fp8_pc_pt_checkpoint> [](#__codelineno-5-2)export VLLM_TEST_MODELOPT_FP8_PB_WO_MODEL_PATH=<path_to_fp8_pb_wo_checkpoint> [](#__codelineno-5-3)pytest -q tests/quantization/test_modelopt.py`

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/online.md "Edit this page")

Online quantization lets you take a BF16/FP16 model and quantize its Linear and MoE weights to lower precision (such as FP8) at load time, without needing a pre-quantized checkpoint or calibration data. Weights are converted during model loading and activations are dynamically scaled during each forward pass.

## Quick Start[¶](#quick-start "Permanent link")

Pass a scheme name to the `quantization` parameter:

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-0-2)[](#__codelineno-0-3)# Per-tensor FP8 quantization (one scale per weight tensor) [](#__codelineno-0-4)llm = LLM("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B", quantization="fp8_per_tensor") [](#__codelineno-0-5)[](#__codelineno-0-6)# Per-block FP8 quantization (128x128 block scaling for weights and 1x128 block scaling for activations) [](#__codelineno-0-7)llm = LLM("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B", quantization="fp8_per_block") [](#__codelineno-0-8)[](#__codelineno-0-9)# MXFP8 quantization for weights and activations [](#__codelineno-0-10)llm = LLM("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B", quantization="mxfp8")`

Or with the CLI:

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --quantization fp8_per_tensor [](#__codelineno-1-2)vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --quantization fp8_per_block [](#__codelineno-1-3)vllm serve meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B --quantization mxfp8`

## Supported Schemes[¶](#supported-schemes "Permanent link")

Scheme

Weight recipe

Activation recipe

Notes

`fp8_per_tensor`

fp8\_e4m3 data, fp32 per-tensor scale

fp8\_e4m3 data, fp32 per-tensor scale

On some GPUs (Ada, Hopper) linear activations use per-token scaling for better performance

`fp8_per_block`

fp8\_e4m3 data, fp32 per-128x128-block scale

fp8\_e4m3 data, fp32 per-1x128-block scale

`mxfp8`

fp8\_e4m3 data, e8m0 per-1x32-block scale

fp8\_e4m3 data, e8m0 per-1x32-block scale

Requires SM 100+ (Blackwell or newer) for w8a8, other GPUs use a w8a16 fallback

## Advanced Configuration[¶](#advanced-configuration "Permanent link")

For fine-grained control, use a `quantization_config` dictionary.

### Schema[¶](#schema "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)quantization_config:   [](#__codelineno-2-2)  linear:    [](#__codelineno-2-3)    weight: <name>      # see QUANT_KEY_NAMES in vllm/config/quantization.py    [](#__codelineno-2-4)    activation: <name>  [](#__codelineno-2-5)  moe:    [](#__codelineno-2-6)    weight: <name>    [](#__codelineno-2-7)    activation: <name>  [](#__codelineno-2-8)  ignore: [<layer-name-or-regex>, ...]`

`linear` and `moe` accept a full `{weight, activation}` dict, or a bare string. A string resolves first against the `--quantization` shorthands (taking the matching layer-kind slot), then against `QUANT_KEY_NAMES` as a weight name. Unset fields fall back to the `--quantization` shorthand's defaults, or for already-quantized checkpoints to whatever the checkpoint declares.

The CLI accepts the same shape as JSON or as dotted keys:

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)vllm serve <model> --quantization-config '{"moe":{"activation":"mxfp8"}}' [](#__codelineno-3-2)vllm serve <model> --quantization-config.moe.activation mxfp8`

### Activation overrides on already-quantized checkpoints[¶](#activation-overrides-on-already-quantized-checkpoints "Permanent link")

For checkpoint-quantized models, `quantization_config` lets you pick an activation format independently of the baked-in weights. The supported overrides are checkpoint-specific; today this is wired up for MXFP4 MoE checkpoints (gpt-oss) where you can opt into FP8 activations:

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)vllm serve openai/gpt-oss-20b --quantization-config.moe.activation mxfp8`

Combine with `--moe-backend` to pin a specific kernel family.

### Separate Schemes for Dense and MoE Layers[¶](#separate-schemes-for-dense-and-moe-layers "Permanent link")

You can apply different quantization schemes to dense linear layers and MoE expert layers via the `linear` and `moe` fields. Each accepts either a full spec dict, or a bare string naming an online shorthand (e.g. `"fp8_per_block"`) or weight format (e.g. `"fp8_per_block_static"`); fields not set fall back to the shorthand defaults.

`[](#__codelineno-5-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-5-2)[](#__codelineno-5-3)# Linear: per-block FP8; MoE: per-tensor FP8 (inherited from the shorthand) [](#__codelineno-5-4)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-5-5)    "ibm-granite/granite-3.0-1b-a400m-base",    [](#__codelineno-5-6)    quantization="fp8_per_tensor",    [](#__codelineno-5-7)    quantization_config={        [](#__codelineno-5-8)        "linear": "fp8_per_block",    [](#__codelineno-5-9)    }, [](#__codelineno-5-10))`

Or,

`[](#__codelineno-6-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-6-2)[](#__codelineno-6-3)# Linear: per-tensor FP8 (inherited); MoE: per-block FP8 [](#__codelineno-6-4)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-6-5)    "ibm-granite/granite-3.0-1b-a400m-base",    [](#__codelineno-6-6)    quantization="fp8_per_tensor",    [](#__codelineno-6-7)    quantization_config={        [](#__codelineno-6-8)        "moe": "fp8_per_block",    [](#__codelineno-6-9)    }, [](#__codelineno-6-10))`

### Excluding Layers from Quantization[¶](#excluding-layers-from-quantization "Permanent link")

Use the `ignore` parameter to skip specific layers. It accepts exact layer names and regex patterns (prefixed with `re:`):

`[](#__codelineno-7-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-7-2)[](#__codelineno-7-3)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-7-4)    "ibm-granite/granite-3.0-1b-a400m-base",    [](#__codelineno-7-5)    quantization="fp8_per_tensor",    [](#__codelineno-7-6)    quantization_config={        [](#__codelineno-7-7)        "ignore": [            [](#__codelineno-7-8)            # exact layer name            [](#__codelineno-7-9)            "model.layers.1.self_attn.o_proj",            [](#__codelineno-7-10)            # regex: skip all QKV projections            [](#__codelineno-7-11)            "re:.*[qkv]_proj",        [](#__codelineno-7-12)        ],    [](#__codelineno-7-13)    }, [](#__codelineno-7-14))`

Note

For fused layers (e.g., `qkv_proj` which fuses `q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj`), the ignore pattern must match the **unfused** shard names (`q_proj`, `k_proj`, `v_proj`), not the fused name.

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/quantized_kvcache.md "Edit this page")

## FP8 KV Cache Overview[¶](#fp8-kv-cache-overview "Permanent link")

Efficient memory usage is crucial for working with large language models. Quantizing the KV (Key-Value) cache to FP8 format can significantly reduce its memory footprint. This optimization enables you to store more tokens in memory, leading to improved throughput and support for longer context windows.

> **Note:** When using the Flash Attention 3 backend with FP8 KV cache, attention operations are also performed in the quantized (FP8) domain. In this configuration, queries are quantized to FP8 in addition to keys and values.

### Supported FP8 KV-Cache Quantization Schemes[¶](#supported-fp8-kv-cache-quantization-schemes "Permanent link")

vLLM supports two main quantization strategies for the FP8 KV-cache:

-   **Per-tensor quantization:**  
    A single scale is applied for each Q, K, and V tensor individually. (`q/k/v_scale = [1]`)
-   **Per-attention-head quantization:**  
    Each scale corresponds to an attention head: `q_scale = [num_heads]`, `k/v_scale = [num_kv_heads]`.

> **Note:**  
> Per-attention-head quantization is currently available **only with the Flash Attention backend** and requires the calibration pathway provided by **llm-compressor**.

### Scale Calibration Approaches[¶](#scale-calibration-approaches "Permanent link")

You can configure how the quantization scales are computed in vLLM using three different approaches:

1.  **No calibration (default scales):**  
    All quantization scales are set to `1.0`.  
    _Configure with:_  
    
    `[](#__codelineno-0-1)kv_cache_dtype="fp8" [](#__codelineno-0-2)calculate_kv_scales=False`
    
2.  **Random token calibration (on-the-fly):**  
    Scales are automatically estimated from a single batch of random tokens during warmup and then fixed.  
    _Configure with:_  
    
    `[](#__codelineno-1-1)kv_cache_dtype="fp8" [](#__codelineno-1-2)calculate_kv_scales=True`
    
3.  **\[Recommended\] Calibration with a dataset (via llm-compressor):**  
    Scales are estimated using a curated calibration dataset for maximum accuracy.  
    This requires the [llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor) library.  
    _See example below!_
    

#### Additional `kv_cache_dtype` Options[¶](#additional-kv_cache_dtype-options "Permanent link")

-   `kv_cache_dtype="auto"`: Use the model's default data type
-   `kv_cache_dtype="fp8_e4m3"`: Supported on CUDA 11.8+ and ROCm (AMD GPUs)
-   `kv_cache_dtype="fp8_e5m2"`: Supported on CUDA 11.8+

* * *

## Examples[¶](#examples "Permanent link")

### 1\. No Calibration (`kv_cache_dtype="fp8"`, `calculate_kv_scales=False`)[¶](#1-no-calibration-kv_cache_dtypefp8-calculate_kv_scalesfalse "Permanent link")

All quantization scales are set to 1.0.

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-2-2)[](#__codelineno-2-3)sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.7, top_p=0.8) [](#__codelineno-2-4)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-2-5)    model="meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf",    [](#__codelineno-2-6)    kv_cache_dtype="fp8",    [](#__codelineno-2-7)    calculate_kv_scales=False, [](#__codelineno-2-8)) [](#__codelineno-2-9)prompt = "London is the capital of" [](#__codelineno-2-10)out = llm.generate(prompt, sampling_params)[0].outputs[0].text [](#__codelineno-2-11)print(out)`

* * *

### 2\. Random Token Calibration (`kv_cache_dtype="fp8"`, `calculate_kv_scales=True`)[¶](#2-random-token-calibration-kv_cache_dtypefp8-calculate_kv_scalestrue "Permanent link")

Scales are automatically estimated from a single batch of tokens during warmup.

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-3-2)[](#__codelineno-3-3)sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.7, top_p=0.8) [](#__codelineno-3-4)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-3-5)    model="meta-llama/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf",    [](#__codelineno-3-6)    kv_cache_dtype="fp8",    [](#__codelineno-3-7)    calculate_kv_scales=True, [](#__codelineno-3-8)) [](#__codelineno-3-9)prompt = "London is the capital of" [](#__codelineno-3-10)out = llm.generate(prompt, sampling_params)[0].outputs[0].text [](#__codelineno-3-11)print(out)`

* * *

### 3\. **\[Recommended\] Calibration Using a Dataset (with `llm-compressor`)**[¶](#3-recommended-calibration-using-a-dataset-with-llm-compressor "Permanent link")

For the highest-quality quantization, we recommend calibrating against a dataset using `llm-compressor`. This enables advanced strategies such as per-attention-head quantization.

#### Install the required package[¶](#install-the-required-package "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)pip install llmcompressor`

#### Example: Quantize Llama Attention & KV Cache to FP8[¶](#example-quantize-llama-attention-kv-cache-to-fp8 "Permanent link")

`[](#__codelineno-5-1)""" [](#__codelineno-5-2)Quantize Llama attention + KV cache to FP8 (choose either 'tensor' or 'attn_head' strategy) [](#__codelineno-5-3)using llm-compressor one-shot calibration. # page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/quark.md "Edit this page")

Quantization can effectively reduce memory and bandwidth usage, accelerate computation and improve throughput while with minimal accuracy loss. vLLM can leverage [Quark](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/), the flexible and powerful quantization toolkit, to produce performant quantized models to run on AMD GPUs. Quark has specialized support for quantizing large language models with weight, activation and kv-cache quantization and cutting-edge quantization algorithms like AWQ, GPTQ, Rotation and SmoothQuant.

## Quark Installation[¶](#quark-installation "Permanent link")

Before quantizing models, you need to install Quark. The latest release of Quark can be installed with pip:

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)pip install amd-quark`

You can refer to [Quark installation guide](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/install.html) for more installation details.

Additionally, install `vllm` and `lm-evaluation-harness` for evaluation:

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)pip install vllm "lm-eval[api]>=0.4.12"`

## Quantization Process[¶](#quantization-process "Permanent link")

After installing Quark, we will use an example to illustrate how to use Quark. The Quark quantization process can be listed for 5 steps as below:

1.  Load the model
2.  Prepare the calibration dataloader
3.  Set the quantization configuration
4.  Quantize the model and export
5.  Evaluation in vLLM

### 1\. Load the Model[¶](#1-load-the-model "Permanent link")

Quark uses [Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/index) to fetch model and tokenizer.

Code

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM [](#__codelineno-2-2)[](#__codelineno-2-3)MODEL_ID = "meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf" [](#__codelineno-2-4)MAX_SEQ_LEN = 512 [](#__codelineno-2-5)[](#__codelineno-2-6)model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(     [](#__codelineno-2-7)    MODEL_ID,    [](#__codelineno-2-8)    device_map="auto",    [](#__codelineno-2-9)    dtype="auto", [](#__codelineno-2-10)) [](#__codelineno-2-11)model.eval() [](#__codelineno-2-12)[](#__codelineno-2-13)tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID, model_max_length=MAX_SEQ_LEN) [](#__codelineno-2-14)tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token`

### 2\. Prepare the Calibration Dataloader[¶](#2-prepare-the-calibration-dataloader "Permanent link")

Quark uses the [PyTorch Dataloader](https://pytorch.org/tutorials/beginner/basics/data_tutorial.html) to load calibration data. For more details about how to use calibration datasets efficiently, please refer to [Adding Calibration Datasets](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/pytorch/calibration_datasets.html).

Code

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from datasets import load_dataset [](#__codelineno-3-2)from torch.utils.data import DataLoader [](#__codelineno-3-3)[](#__codelineno-3-4)BATCH_SIZE = 1 [](#__codelineno-3-5)NUM_CALIBRATION_DATA = 512 [](#__codelineno-3-6)[](#__codelineno-3-7)# Load the dataset and get calibration data. [](#__codelineno-3-8)dataset = load_dataset("mit-han-lab/pile-val-backup", split="validation") [](#__codelineno-3-9)text_data = dataset["text"][:NUM_CALIBRATION_DATA] [](#__codelineno-3-10)[](#__codelineno-3-11)tokenized_outputs = tokenizer(     [](#__codelineno-3-12)    text_data,    [](#__codelineno-3-13)    return_tensors="pt",    [](#__codelineno-3-14)    padding=True,    [](#__codelineno-3-15)    truncation=True,    [](#__codelineno-3-16)    max_length=MAX_SEQ_LEN, [](#__codelineno-3-17)) [](#__codelineno-3-18)calib_dataloader = DataLoader(     [](#__codelineno-3-19)    tokenized_outputs['input_ids'],    [](#__codelineno-3-20)    batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,    [](#__codelineno-3-21)    drop_last=True, [](#__codelineno-3-22))`

### 3\. Set the Quantization Configuration[¶](#3-set-the-quantization-configuration "Permanent link")

We need to set the quantization configuration, you can check [quark config guide](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/pytorch/user_guide_config_description.html) for further details. Here we use FP8 per-tensor quantization on weight, activation, kv-cache and the quantization algorithm is AutoSmoothQuant.

Note

Note the quantization algorithm needs a JSON config file and the config file is located in [Quark Pytorch examples](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/pytorch/pytorch_examples.html), under the directory `examples/torch/language_modeling/llm_ptq/models`. For example, AutoSmoothQuant config file for Llama is `examples/torch/language_modeling/llm_ptq/models/llama/autosmoothquant_config.json`.

Code

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)from quark.torch.quantization import (Config, QuantizationConfig,                                     [](#__codelineno-4-2)                                    FP8E4M3PerTensorSpec,                                    [](#__codelineno-4-3)                                    load_quant_algo_config_from_file) [](#__codelineno-4-4)[](#__codelineno-4-5)# Define fp8/per-tensor/static spec. [](#__codelineno-4-6)FP8_PER_TENSOR_SPEC = FP8E4M3PerTensorSpec(     [](#__codelineno-4-7)    observer_method="min_max",    [](#__codelineno-4-8)    is_dynamic=False, [](#__codelineno-4-9)).to_quantization_spec() [](#__codelineno-4-10)[](#__codelineno-4-11)# Define global quantization config, input tensors and weight apply FP8_PER_TENSOR_SPEC. [](#__codelineno-4-12)global_quant_config = QuantizationConfig(     [](#__codelineno-4-13)    input_tensors=FP8_PER_TENSOR_SPEC,    [](#__codelineno-4-14)    weight=FP8_PER_TENSOR_SPEC, [](#__codelineno-4-15)) [](#__codelineno-4-16)[](#__codelineno-4-17)# Define quantization config for kv-cache layers, output tensors apply FP8_PER_TENSOR_SPEC. [](#__codelineno-4-18)KV_CACHE_SPEC = FP8_PER_TENSOR_SPEC [](#__codelineno-4-19)kv_cache_layer_names_for_llama = ["*k_proj", "*v_proj"] [](#__codelineno-4-20)kv_cache_quant_config = {     [](#__codelineno-4-21)    name: QuantizationConfig(        [](#__codelineno-4-22)        input_tensors=global_quant_config.input_tensors,        [](#__codelineno-4-23)        weight=global_quant_config.weight,        [](#__codelineno-4-24)        output_tensors=KV_CACHE_SPEC,    [](#__codelineno-4-25)    )    [](#__codelineno-4-26)    for name in kv_cache_layer_names_for_llama [](#__codelineno-4-27)} [](#__codelineno-4-28)layer_quant_config = kv_cache_quant_config.copy() [](#__codelineno-4-29)[](#__codelineno-4-30)# Define algorithm config by config file. [](#__codelineno-4-31)LLAMA_AUTOSMOOTHQUANT_CONFIG_FILE = "examples/torch/language_modeling/llm_ptq/models/llama/autosmoothquant_config.json" [](#__codelineno-4-32)algo_config = load_quant_algo_config_from_file(LLAMA_AUTOSMOOTHQUANT_CONFIG_FILE) [](#__codelineno-4-33)[](#__codelineno-4-34)EXCLUDE_LAYERS = ["lm_head"] [](#__codelineno-4-35)quant_config = Config(     [](#__codelineno-4-36)    global_quant_config=global_quant_config,    [](#__codelineno-4-37)    layer_quant_config=layer_quant_config,    [](#__codelineno-4-38)    kv_cache_quant_config=kv_cache_quant_config,    [](#__codelineno-4-39)    exclude=EXCLUDE_LAYERS,    [](#__codelineno-4-40)    algo_config=algo_config, [](#__codelineno-4-41))`

### 4\. Quantize the Model and Export[¶](#4-quantize-the-model-and-export "Permanent link")

Then we can apply the quantization. After quantizing, we need to freeze the quantized model first before exporting. Note that we need to export model with format of HuggingFace `safetensors`, you can refer to [HuggingFace format exporting](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/pytorch/export/quark_export_hf.html) for more exporting format details.

Code

`[](#__codelineno-5-1)import torch [](#__codelineno-5-2)from quark.torch import ModelQuantizer, ModelExporter [](#__codelineno-5-3)from quark.torch.export import ExporterConfig, JsonExporterConfig [](#__codelineno-5-4)[](#__codelineno-5-5)# Apply quantization. [](#__codelineno-5-6)quantizer = ModelQuantizer(quant_config) [](#__codelineno-5-7)quant_model = quantizer.quantize_model(model, calib_dataloader) [](#__codelineno-5-8)[](#__codelineno-5-9)# Freeze quantized model to export. [](#__codelineno-5-10)freezed_model = quantizer.freeze(model) [](#__codelineno-5-11)[](#__codelineno-5-12)# Define export config. [](#__codelineno-5-13)LLAMA_KV_CACHE_GROUP = ["*k_proj", "*v_proj"] [](#__codelineno-5-14)export_config = ExporterConfig(json_export_config=JsonExporterConfig()) [](#__codelineno-5-15)export_config.json_export_config.kv_cache_group = LLAMA_KV_CACHE_GROUP [](#__codelineno-5-16)[](#__codelineno-5-17)# Model: Llama-2-70b-chat-hf-w-fp8-a-fp8-kvcache-fp8-pertensor-autosmoothquant [](#__codelineno-5-18)EXPORT_DIR = MODEL_ID.split("/")[1] + "-w-fp8-a-fp8-kvcache-fp8-pertensor-autosmoothquant" [](#__codelineno-5-19)exporter = ModelExporter(config=export_config, export_dir=EXPORT_DIR) [](#__codelineno-5-20)with torch.no_grad():     [](#__codelineno-5-21)    exporter.export_safetensors_model(        [](#__codelineno-5-22)        freezed_model,        [](#__codelineno-5-23)        quant_config=quant_config,        [](#__codelineno-5-24)        tokenizer=tokenizer,    [](#__codelineno-5-25)    )`

### 5\. Evaluation in vLLM[¶](#5-evaluation-in-vllm "Permanent link")

Now, you can load and run the Quark quantized model directly through the LLM entrypoint:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-6-1)from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams [](#__codelineno-6-2)[](#__codelineno-6-3)# Sample prompts. [](#__codelineno-6-4)prompts = [     [](#__codelineno-6-5)    "Hello, my name is",    [](#__codelineno-6-6)    "The president of the United States is",    [](#__codelineno-6-7)    "The capital of France is",    [](#__codelineno-6-8)    "The future of AI is", [](#__codelineno-6-9)] [](#__codelineno-6-10)# Create a sampling params object. [](#__codelineno-6-11)sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.8, top_p=0.95) [](#__codelineno-6-12)[](#__codelineno-6-13)# Create an LLM. [](#__codelineno-6-14)llm = LLM(     [](#__codelineno-6-15)    model="Llama-2-70b-chat-hf-w-fp8-a-fp8-kvcache-fp8-pertensor-autosmoothquant",    [](#__codelineno-6-16)    kv_cache_dtype="fp8",    [](#__codelineno-6-17)    quantization="quark", [](#__codelineno-6-18)) [](#__codelineno-6-19)# Generate texts from the prompts. The output is a list of RequestOutput objects [](#__codelineno-6-20)# that contain the prompt, generated text, and other information. Or, you can use `lm_eval` to evaluate accuracy:

`[](#__codelineno-7-1)lm_eval --model vllm \   [](#__codelineno-7-2)  --model_args pretrained=Llama-2-70b-chat-hf-w-fp8-a-fp8-kvcache-fp8-pertensor-autosmoothquant,kv_cache_dtype='fp8',quantization='quark' \  [](#__codelineno-7-3)  --tasks gsm8k`

## Quark Quantization Script[¶](#quark-quantization-script "Permanent link")

In addition to the example of Python API above, Quark also offers a [quantization script](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/pytorch/example_quark_torch_llm_ptq.html) to quantize large language models more conveniently. It supports quantizing models with variety of different quantization schemes and optimization algorithms. It can export the quantized model and run evaluation tasks on the fly. With the script, the example above can be:

`[](#__codelineno-8-1)python3 quantize_quark.py --model_dir meta-llama/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf \                           [](#__codelineno-8-2)                          --output_dir /path/to/output \                          [](#__codelineno-8-3)                          --quant_scheme w_fp8_a_fp8 \                          [](#__codelineno-8-4)                          --kv_cache_dtype fp8 \                          [](#__codelineno-8-5)                          --quant_algo autosmoothquant \                          [](#__codelineno-8-6)                          --num_calib_data 512 \                          [](#__codelineno-8-7)                          --model_export hf_format \                          [](#__codelineno-8-8)                          --tasks gsm8k`

## Using OCP MX (MXFP4, MXFP6) models[¶](#using-ocp-mx-mxfp4-mxfp6-models "Permanent link")

vLLM supports loading MXFP4 and MXFP6 models quantized offline through AMD Quark, compliant with [Open Compute Project (OCP) specification](https://www.opencompute.org/documents/ocp-microscaling-formats-mx-v1-0-spec-final-pdf).

The scheme currently only supports dynamic quantization for activations.

Example usage, after installing the latest AMD Quark release:

`[](#__codelineno-9-1)vllm serve fxmarty/qwen_1.5-moe-a2.7b-mxfp4 --tensor-parallel-size 1 [](#__codelineno-9-2)# or, for a model using fp6 activations and fp4 weights: [](#__codelineno-9-3)vllm serve fxmarty/qwen1.5_moe_a2.7b_chat_w_fp4_a_fp6_e2m3 --tensor-parallel-size 1`

A simulation of the matrix multiplication execution in MXFP4/MXFP6 can be run on devices that do not support OCP MX operations natively (e.g. AMD Instinct MI325, MI300 and MI250), dequantizing weights from FP4/FP6 to half precision on the fly, using a fused kernel. This is useful e.g. to evaluate FP4/FP6 models using vLLM, or alternatively to benefit from the ~2.5-4x memory savings (compared to float16 and bfloat16).

To generate offline models quantized using MXFP4 data type, the easiest approach is to use AMD Quark's [quantization script](https://quark.docs.amd.com/latest/pytorch/example_quark_torch_llm_ptq.html), as an example:

`[](#__codelineno-10-1)python quantize_quark.py --model_dir Qwen/Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B-Chat \     [](#__codelineno-10-2)    --quant_scheme w_mxfp4_a_mxfp4 \    [](#__codelineno-10-3)    --output_dir qwen_1.5-moe-a2.7b-mxfp4 \    [](#__codelineno-10-4)    --skip_evaluation \    [](#__codelineno-10-5)    --model_export hf_format \    [](#__codelineno-10-6)    --group_size 32`

The current integration supports [all combination of FP4, FP6\_E3M2, FP6\_E2M3](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/layers/quantization/utils/ocp_mx_utils.py) used for either weights or activations.

## Using Quark Quantized layerwise Auto Mixed Precision (AMP) Models[¶](#using-quark-quantized-layerwise-auto-mixed-precision-amp-models "Permanent link")

vLLM also supports loading layerwise mixed precision model quantized using AMD Quark. Currently, mixed scheme of {MXFP4, FP8} is supported, where FP8 here denotes for FP8 per-tensor scheme. More mixed precision schemes are planned to be supported in a near future, including

-   Unquantized Linear and/or MoE layer(s) as an option for each layer, i.e., mixed of {MXFP4, FP8, BF16/FP16}
-   MXFP6 quantization extension, i.e., {MXFP4, MXFP6, FP8, BF16/FP16}

Although one can maximize serving throughput using the lowest precision supported on a given device (e.g. MXFP4 for AMD Instinct MI355, FP8 for AMD Instinct MI300), these aggressive schemes can be detrimental to accuracy recovering from quantization on target tasks. Mixed precision allows to strike a balance between maximizing accuracy and throughput.

There are two steps to generate and deploy a mixed precision model quantized with AMD Quark, as shown below.

### 1\. Quantize a model using mixed precision in AMD Quark[¶](#1-quantize-a-model-using-mixed-precision-in-amd-quark "Permanent link")

Firstly, the layerwise mixed-precision configuration for a given LLM model is searched and then quantized using AMD Quark. We will provide a detailed tutorial with Quark APIs later.

As examples, we provide some ready-to-use quantized mixed precision model to show the usage in vLLM and the accuracy benefits. They are:

-   amd/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf-WMXFP4FP8-AMXFP4FP8-AMP-KVFP8
-   amd/Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1-WMXFP4FP8-AMXFP4FP8-AMP-KVFP8
-   amd/Qwen3-8B-WMXFP4FP8-AMXFP4FP8-AMP-KVFP8

### 2\. inference the quantized mixed precision model in vLLM[¶](#2-inference-the-quantized-mixed-precision-model-in-vllm "Permanent link")

Models quantized with AMD Quark using mixed precision can natively be reload in vLLM, and e.g. evaluated using lm-evaluation-harness as follows:

`[](#__codelineno-11-1)lm_eval --model vllm \     [](#__codelineno-11-2)    --model_args pretrained=amd/Llama-2-70b-chat-hf-WMXFP4FP8-AMXFP4FP8-AMP-KVFP8,tensor_parallel_size=4,dtype=auto,gpu_memory_utilization=0.8,trust_remote_code=False \    [](#__codelineno-11-3)    --tasks mmlu \    [](#__codelineno-11-4)    --batch_size auto`

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/torchao.md "Edit this page")

TorchAO is an architecture optimization library for PyTorch, it provides high performance dtypes, optimization techniques and kernels for inference and training, featuring composability with native PyTorch features like torch.compile, FSDP etc.. Some benchmark numbers can be found [here](https://github.com/pytorch/ao/tree/main/torchao/quantization#benchmarks).

We recommend installing the latest torchao nightly with

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)# Install the latest TorchAO nightly build [](#__codelineno-0-2)# Choose the CUDA version that matches your system (cu126, cu128, etc.) [](#__codelineno-0-3)pip install \     [](#__codelineno-0-4)    --pre torchao>=10.0.0 \    [](#__codelineno-0-5)    --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/nightly/cu126`

## Quantizing HuggingFace Models[¶](#quantizing-huggingface-models "Permanent link")

You can quantize your own huggingface model with torchao, e.g. [transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/quantization/torchao) and [diffusers](https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/en/quantization/torchao), and save the checkpoint to huggingface hub like [this](https://huggingface.co/jerryzh168/llama3-8b-int8wo) with the following example code:

Code

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)import torch [](#__codelineno-1-2)from transformers import TorchAoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer [](#__codelineno-1-3)from torchao.quantization import Int8WeightOnlyConfig [](#__codelineno-1-4)[](#__codelineno-1-5)model_name = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B" [](#__codelineno-1-6)quantization_config = TorchAoConfig(Int8WeightOnlyConfig()) [](#__codelineno-1-7)quantized_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(     [](#__codelineno-1-8)    model_name,    [](#__codelineno-1-9)    dtype="auto",    [](#__codelineno-1-10)    device_map="auto",    [](#__codelineno-1-11)    quantization_config=quantization_config [](#__codelineno-1-12)) [](#__codelineno-1-13)tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name) [](#__codelineno-1-14)input_text = "What are we having for dinner?" [](#__codelineno-1-15)input_ids = tokenizer(input_text, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda") [](#__codelineno-1-16)[](#__codelineno-1-17)hub_repo = # YOUR HUB REPO ID [](#__codelineno-1-18)tokenizer.push_to_hub(hub_repo) [](#__codelineno-1-19)quantized_model.push_to_hub(hub_repo, safe_serialization=False)`

Alternatively, you can use the [TorchAO Quantization space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/medmekk/TorchAO_Quantization) for quantizing models with a simple UI.

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/llm_compressor/README.md "Edit this page")

[LLM Compressor](https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/llm-compressor/en/latest/) is a library for optimizing models for deployment with vLLM. It provides a comprehensive set of quantization algorithms, including support for techniques such as FP4, FP8, INT8, and INT4 quantization.

## Why use LLM Compressor?[¶](#why-use-llm-compressor "Permanent link")

Modern LLMs often contain billions of parameters stored in 16-bit or 32-bit floating point, requiring substantial GPU memory and limiting deployment options. Quantization lowers memory requirements while maintaining inference output quality by reducing the precision of model weights and activations to smaller data types.

LLM Compressor provides the following benefits:

-   **Reduced memory footprint**: Run larger models on smaller GPUs.
-   **Lower inference costs**: Serve more concurrent users per GPU, directly reducing the cost per query in production deployments.
-   **Faster inference**: Smaller data types mean less memory bandwidth consumed, which often translates to higher throughput, especially for memory-bound workloads.

LLM Compressor handles the complexity of quantization, calibration, and format conversion, producing models ready for immediate use with vLLM.

## Key features[¶](#key-features "Permanent link")

-   **Multiple Quantization Algorithms**: Support for AWQ, GPTQ, AutoRound, and Round-to-Nearest. Also includes support for QuIP and SpinQuant-style transforms as well as KV cache and attention quantization.
-   **Multiple Quantization Methods**: Support for FP8, INT8, INT4, NVFP4, MXFP4, and mixed-precision quantization
-   **One-Shot Quantization**: Quantize models quickly with minimal calibration data
-   **vLLM Integration**: Seamlessly deploy quantized models with vLLM using the compressed-tensors format
-   **Hugging Face Compatibility**: Works with models from the Hugging Face Hub

## Resources[¶](#resources "Permanent link")

-   [LLM Compressor examples](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/tree/main/examples)
-   [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor)

---

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/llm_compressor/fp8.md "Edit this page")

vLLM supports FP8 (8-bit floating point) weight and activation quantization using hardware acceleration on GPUs such as Nvidia H100 and AMD MI300x. Currently, only Hopper and Ada Lovelace GPUs are officially supported for W8A8. Turing/Ampere GPUs are supported for W8A16 (weight-only FP8) utilizing Marlin kernels. Quantization of models with FP8 allows for a 2x reduction in model memory requirements and up to a 1.6x improvement in throughput with minimal impact on accuracy.

Please visit the HF collection of [quantized FP8 checkpoints of popular LLMs ready to use with vLLM](https://huggingface.co/collections/neuralmagic/fp8-llms-for-vllm-666742ed2b78b7ac8df13127).

The FP8 types typically supported in hardware have two distinct representations, each useful in different scenarios:

-   **E4M3**: Consists of 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits, and 3 bits of mantissa. It can store values up to +/-448 and `nan`.
-   **E5M2**: Consists of 1 sign bit, 5 exponent bits, and 2 bits of mantissa. It can store values up to +/-57344, +/- `inf`, and `nan`. The tradeoff for the increased dynamic range is lower precision of the stored values.

Note

FP8 computation is supported on NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability >= 8.9 (Ada Lovelace, Hopper). FP8 models will run on compute capability >= 7.5 (Turing) as weight-only W8A16, utilizing FP8 Marlin.

## Installation[¶](#installation "Permanent link")

To produce performant FP8 quantized models with vLLM, you'll need to install the [llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/) library:

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)(venv-llm-compressor) pip install llmcompressor`

Additionally, install `vllm` and `lm-evaluation-harness` for evaluation:

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)(venv-vllm) pip install vllm "lm-eval[api]>=0.4.12"`

Please use separate environments for vLLM and llm-compressor as they might not work together.

## Quantization Process[¶](#quantization-process "Permanent link")

The quantization process involves three main steps:

1.  Loading the model
2.  Applying quantization
3.  Evaluating accuracy in vLLM

### 1\. Loading the Model[¶](#1-loading-the-model "Permanent link")

Load your model and tokenizer using the standard `transformers` AutoModel classes:

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM [](#__codelineno-2-2)[](#__codelineno-2-3)MODEL_ID = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct" [](#__codelineno-2-4)model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(     [](#__codelineno-2-5)    MODEL_ID,    [](#__codelineno-2-6)    device_map="auto",    [](#__codelineno-2-7)    dtype="auto", [](#__codelineno-2-8)) [](#__codelineno-2-9)tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)`

### 2\. Applying Quantization[¶](#2-applying-quantization "Permanent link")

For FP8 quantization, we can recover accuracy with simple RTN quantization. We recommend targeting all `Linear` layers using the `FP8_DYNAMIC` scheme, which uses:

-   Static, per-channel quantization on the weights
-   Dynamic, per-token quantization on the activations

Since simple RTN does not require data for weight quantization and the activations are quantized dynamically, we do not need any calibration data for this quantization flow.

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from llmcompressor import oneshot [](#__codelineno-3-2)from llmcompressor.modifiers.quantization import QuantizationModifier [](#__codelineno-3-3)[](#__codelineno-3-4)# Configure the simple PTQ quantization [](#__codelineno-3-5)recipe = QuantizationModifier(     [](#__codelineno-3-6)    targets="Linear",    [](#__codelineno-3-7)    scheme="FP8_DYNAMIC",    [](#__codelineno-3-8)    ignore=["lm_head"], [](#__codelineno-3-9)) [](#__codelineno-3-10)[](#__codelineno-3-11)# Apply the quantization algorithm. [](#__codelineno-3-12)oneshot(model=model, recipe=recipe) [](#__codelineno-3-13)[](#__codelineno-3-14)# Save the model: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-FP8-Dynamic [](#__codelineno-3-15)SAVE_DIR = MODEL_ID.split("/")[1] + "-FP8-Dynamic" [](#__codelineno-3-16)model.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR) [](#__codelineno-3-17)tokenizer.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR)`

### 3\. Evaluating Accuracy[¶](#3-evaluating-accuracy "Permanent link")

Load and run the model in `vllm`:

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-4-2)[](#__codelineno-4-3)llm = LLM("./Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-FP8-Dynamic") [](#__codelineno-4-4)result = llm.generate("Hello my name is") [](#__codelineno-4-5)print(result[0].outputs[0].text)`

Evaluate accuracy with `lm_eval` (for example on 250 samples of `gsm8k`):

Note

Quantized models can be sensitive to the presence of the `bos` token. `lm_eval` does not add a `bos` token by default, so make sure to include the `add_bos_token=True` argument when running your evaluations.

`[](#__codelineno-5-1)MODEL=$PWD/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-FP8-Dynamic [](#__codelineno-5-2)lm_eval \   [](#__codelineno-5-3)  --model vllm \  [](#__codelineno-5-4)  --model_args pretrained=$MODEL,add_bos_token=True \  [](#__codelineno-5-5)  --tasks gsm8k  --num_fewshot 5 --batch_size auto --limit 250`

Here's an example of the resulting scores:

`[](#__codelineno-6-1)|Tasks|Version|     Filter     |n-shot|  Metric   |   |Value|   |Stderr| [](#__codelineno-6-2)| --- |------:| -------------- |-----:| --------- | - |----:| - |-----:| [](#__codelineno-6-3)|gsm8k|      3|flexible-extract|     5|exact_match|↑  |0.768|±  |0.0268| [](#__codelineno-6-4)|     |       |strict-match    |     5|exact_match|↑  |0.768|±  |0.0268|`

## Troubleshooting and Support[¶](#troubleshooting-and-support "Permanent link")

If you encounter any issues or have feature requests, please open an issue on the [vllm-project/llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues) GitHub repository.

## Online Dynamic Quantization[¶](#online-dynamic-quantization "Permanent link")

Dynamic quantization of an original precision BF16/FP16 model to FP8 can be achieved with vLLM without any calibration data required. You can enable the feature by specifying `--quantization="fp8"` in the command line or setting `quantization="fp8"` in the LLM constructor.

In this mode, all Linear modules (except for the final `lm_head`) have their weights quantized down to FP8\_E4M3 precision with a per-tensor scale. Activations have their minimum and maximum values calculated during each forward pass to provide a dynamic per-tensor scale for high accuracy. As a result, latency improvements are limited in this mode.

`[](#__codelineno-7-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-7-2)[](#__codelineno-7-3)llm = LLM("facebook/opt-125m", quantization="fp8") [](#__codelineno-7-4)# INFO 06-10 17:55:42 model_runner.py:157] Loading model weights took 0.1550 GB [](#__codelineno-7-5)result = llm.generate("Hello, my name is") [](#__codelineno-7-6)print(result[0].outputs[0].text)`

# page

[](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/edit/main/docs/features/quantization/llm_compressor/int4.md "Edit this page")

vLLM supports quantizing weights to INT4 for memory savings and inference acceleration. This quantization method is particularly useful for reducing model size and maintaining low latency in workloads with low queries per second (QPS).

Please visit the HF collection of [quantized INT4 checkpoints of popular LLMs ready to use with vLLM](https://huggingface.co/collections/neuralmagic/int4-llms-for-vllm-668ec34bf3c9fa45f857df2c).

Note

INT4 computation is supported on NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability > 8.0 (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, Hopper, Blackwell).

## Prerequisites[¶](#prerequisites "Permanent link")

To use INT4 quantization with vLLM, you'll need to install the [llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/) library:

`[](#__codelineno-0-1)(venv-llm-compressor) pip install llmcompressor`

Additionally, install `vllm` and `lm-evaluation-harness` for evaluation:

`[](#__codelineno-1-1)(venv-vllm) pip install vllm "lm-eval[api]>=0.4.12"`

Please use separate environments for vLLM and llm-compressor as they might not work together.

## Quantization Process[¶](#quantization-process "Permanent link")

The quantization process involves four main steps:

1.  Loading the model
2.  Preparing calibration data
3.  Applying quantization
4.  Evaluating accuracy in vLLM

### 1\. Loading the Model[¶](#1-loading-the-model "Permanent link")

Load your model and tokenizer using the standard `transformers` AutoModel classes:

`[](#__codelineno-2-1)from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM [](#__codelineno-2-2)[](#__codelineno-2-3)MODEL_ID = "meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct" [](#__codelineno-2-4)model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(     [](#__codelineno-2-5)    MODEL_ID,    [](#__codelineno-2-6)    device_map="auto",    [](#__codelineno-2-7)    dtype="auto", [](#__codelineno-2-8)) [](#__codelineno-2-9)tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)`

### 2\. Preparing Calibration Data[¶](#2-preparing-calibration-data "Permanent link")

When quantizing weights to INT4, you need sample data to estimate the weight updates and calibrated scales. It's best to use calibration data that closely matches your deployment data. For a general-purpose instruction-tuned model, you can use a dataset like `ultrachat`:

`[](#__codelineno-3-1)from datasets import load_dataset [](#__codelineno-3-2)[](#__codelineno-3-3)NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES = 512 [](#__codelineno-3-4)MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH = 2048 [](#__codelineno-3-5)[](#__codelineno-3-6)# Load and preprocess the dataset [](#__codelineno-3-7)ds = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k", split="train_sft") [](#__codelineno-3-8)ds = ds.shuffle(seed=42).select(range(NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES)) [](#__codelineno-3-9)[](#__codelineno-3-10)def preprocess(example):     [](#__codelineno-3-11)    return {"text": tokenizer.apply_chat_template(example["messages"], tokenize=False)} [](#__codelineno-3-12)ds = ds.map(preprocess) [](#__codelineno-3-13)[](#__codelineno-3-14)def tokenize(sample):     [](#__codelineno-3-15)    return tokenizer(sample["text"], padding=False, max_length=MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH, truncation=True, add_special_tokens=False) [](#__codelineno-3-16)ds = ds.map(tokenize, remove_columns=ds.column_names)`

### 3\. Applying Quantization[¶](#3-applying-quantization "Permanent link")

Now, apply the quantization algorithms:

`[](#__codelineno-4-1)from llmcompressor import oneshot [](#__codelineno-4-2)from llmcompressor.modifiers.quantization import GPTQModifier [](#__codelineno-4-3)from llmcompressor.modifiers.smoothquant import SmoothQuantModifier [](#__codelineno-4-4)[](#__codelineno-4-5)# Configure the quantization algorithms [](#__codelineno-4-6)recipe = GPTQModifier(targets="Linear", scheme="W4A16", ignore=["lm_head"]) [](#__codelineno-4-7)[](#__codelineno-4-8)# Apply quantization [](#__codelineno-4-9)oneshot(     [](#__codelineno-4-10)    model=model,    [](#__codelineno-4-11)    dataset=ds,    [](#__codelineno-4-12)    recipe=recipe,    [](#__codelineno-4-13)    max_seq_length=MAX_SEQUENCE_LENGTH,    [](#__codelineno-4-14)    num_calibration_samples=NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES, [](#__codelineno-4-15)) [](#__codelineno-4-16)[](#__codelineno-4-17)# Save the compressed model: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-W4A16-G128 [](#__codelineno-4-18)SAVE_DIR = MODEL_ID.split("/")[1] + "-W4A16-G128" [](#__codelineno-4-19)model.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR, save_compressed=True) [](#__codelineno-4-20)tokenizer.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR)`

This process creates a W4A16 model with weights quantized to 4-bit integers.

### 4\. Evaluating Accuracy[¶](#4-evaluating-accuracy "Permanent link")

After quantization, you can load and run the model in vLLM:

`[](#__codelineno-5-1)from vllm import LLM [](#__codelineno-5-2)[](#__codelineno-5-3)llm = LLM("./Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-W4A16-G128")`

To evaluate accuracy, you can use `lm_eval`:

`[](#__codelineno-6-1)lm_eval --model vllm \   [](#__codelineno-6-2)  --model_args pretrained="./Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-W4A16-G128",add_bos_token=true \  [](#__codelineno-6-3)  --tasks gsm8k \  [](#__codelineno-6-4)  --num_fewshot 5 \  [](#__codelineno-6-5)  --limit 250 \  [](#__codelineno-6-6)  --batch_size 'auto'`

Note

Quantized models can be sensitive to the presence of the `bos` token. Make sure to include the `add_bos_token=True` argument when running evaluations.

## Best Practices[¶](#best-practices "Permanent link")

-   Start with 512 samples for calibration data, and increase if accuracy drops
-   Ensure the calibration data contains a high variety of samples to prevent overfitting towards a specific use case
-   Use a sequence length of 2048 as a starting point
-   Employ the chat template or instruction template that the model was trained with
-   If you've fine-tuned a model, consider using a sample of your training data for calibration
-   Tune key hyperparameters to the quantization algorithm:
    -   `dampening_frac` sets how much influence the GPTQ algorithm has. Lower values can improve accuracy, but can lead to numerical instabilities that cause the algorithm to fail.
    -   `actorder` sets the activation ordering. When compressing the weights of a layer weight, the order in which channels are quantized matters. Setting `actorder="weight"` can improve accuracy without added latency.

The following is an example of an expanded quantization recipe you can tune to your own use case:

`[](#__codelineno-7-1)from compressed_tensors.quantization import (     [](#__codelineno-7-2)    QuantizationArgs,    [](#__codelineno-7-3)    QuantizationScheme,    [](#__codelineno-7-4)    QuantizationStrategy,    [](#__codelineno-7-5)    QuantizationType, [](#__codelineno-7-6)) [](#__codelineno-7-7)recipe = GPTQModifier(     [](#__codelineno-7-8)    targets="Linear",    [](#__codelineno-7-9)    config_groups={        [](#__codelineno-7-10)        "config_group": QuantizationScheme(            [](#__codelineno-7-11)            targets=["Linear"],            [](#__codelineno-7-12)            weights=QuantizationArgs(                [](#__codelineno-7-13)                num_bits=4,                [](#__codelineno-7-14)                type=QuantizationType.INT,                [](#__codelineno-7-15)                strategy=QuantizationStrategy.GROUP,                [](#__codelineno-7-16)                group_size=128,                [](#__codelineno-7-17)                symmetric=True,                [](#__codelineno-7-18)                dynamic=False,                [](#__codelineno-7-19)                actorder="weight",            [](#__codelineno-7-20)            ),        [](#__codelineno-7-21)        ),    [](#__codelineno-7-22)    },    [](#__codelineno-7-23)    ignore=["lm_head"],    [](#__codelineno-7-24)    update_size=NUM_CALIBRATION_SAMPLES,    [](#__codelineno-7-25)    dampening_frac=0.01, [](#__codelineno-7-26))`

## Troubleshooting and Support[¶](#troubleshooting-and-support "Permanent link")

If you encounter any issues or have feature requests, please open an issue on the [vllm-project/llm-compressor](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/issues) GitHub repository. The full INT4 quantization example in `llm-compressor` is available [here](https://github.com/vllm-project/llm-compressor/blob/main/examples/quantization_w4a16/llama3_example.py).
